claims.source: Agencia Peruana de Noticias Andina (Editora Perú), 18 October 2013
claims.text: The office is named Departamento de Investigación de Fenómenos Aéreos Anómalos (DIFAA) and sits under the Dirección de Intereses Aéreos Espaciales (DINAE) of the Fuerza Aérea del Perú. Its reopening and a public reporting channel were announced on 18 October 2013 by the head of DINAE, Coronel FAP Julio Vucetich Abanto, who said the service was acting on an increase in sightings being reported to the media: 'Nos interesa que la población que observa fenómenos aparentemente no convencionales, que le causan extrañeza o preocupación, conozca que existe una institución que hará un adecuado estudio e investigación de su información para darles una respuesta. Esto no ocurría antes.'

claims.source: Agencia Peruana de Noticias Andina (Editora Perú), 18 October 2013
claims.text: DIFAA had been closed for five years before the 2013 reopening, 'a causa de problemas administrativos'. The reopening was announced at an FAP-organised 'Encuentro sobre Fenómenos Aéreos Anómalos' addressed to the Nazca Lines question, at which the invited archaeologist Manuel Aguirre Morales said there is no evidence linking the Nazca lines to UFOs or extraterrestrial presence.

claims.source: Agencia Peruana de Noticias Andina (Editora Perú), 18 October 2013
claims.text: Andina framed the reopening regionally: 'Con la reapertura de la DIFAA, el Perú se coloca a la paridad de países de la región como Chile, Argentina, Uruguay, Brasil y Ecuador.'

Not established in this pass: DIFAA's founding legal instrument, its current name and reporting line, its case output, whether it publishes findings, and whether it has ever had contact with any United States body. No US-Peru link was found and none is asserted.

claims.source: BBC Mundo, 5 February 2014, indexed via Google News
claims.text: BBC Mundo reported on 5 February 2014 under the headline 'Por qué Perú reabrió la oficina de búsqueda de ovnis' that Peru had reopened its official UFO investigation office.

connections.edgeLabel: COMPARISON: a military-hosted office against a civil-aviation-hosted one, in the same region
connections.label: CEFAA / SEFAA - Chilean anomalous aerial phenomena office, Dirección General de Aeronáutica Civil
connections.note: COMPARISON EDGE — no joint work is claimed. Andina names Chile among the regional peers DIFAA's reopening brought Peru level with, and reports Peru's stated posture on cooperation as reserved: it considered itself able to analyse the phenomena independently and would appeal to exchange with neighbours only exceptionally, to compare data. Structurally the two are opposites: DIFAA sits inside the Fuerza Aérea del Perú under DINAE, while CEFAA/SEFAA sits inside Chile's civil aviation authority, the DGAC, and frames the subject as an aviation-safety matter. Tier 2 — the structural contrast is analytic, the Peruvian facts are Andina-sourced and the Chilean facts sit on the cefaa and dgac-chile nodes.

connections.label: Força Aérea Brasileira / Ministério da Aeronáutica
connections.note: COMPARISON EDGE — no institutional contact between the FAP and the FAB is claimed. Peru's state news agency Andina, reporting the reopening on 18 October 2013, closes: 'Con la reapertura de la DIFAA, el Perú se coloca a la paridad de países de la región como Chile, Argentina, Uruguay, Brasil y Ecuador.' Brazil is named by a Peruvian government outlet as the regional benchmark. The same report establishes the office's identity that the peru-uap-office node lacked: the Departamento de Investigación de Fenómenos Aéreos Anómalos (DIFAA), sitting under the Dirección de Intereses Aéreos Espaciales (DINAE), whose head Coronel FAP Julio Vucetich Abanto announced the public reporting channel, the office having been closed for five years 'a causa de problemas administrativos'. The reopening was announced at an FAP-hosted 'Encuentro sobre Fenómenos Aéreos Anómalos' addressing the Nazca Lines question.

connections.label: GEIPAN - Groupe d'Études et d'Informations sur les Phénomènes Aérospatiaux Non identifiés
connections.note: COMPARISON EDGE — no contact is claimed and none was found. DIFAA is hosted by an air force; GEIPAN is hosted by a civil space agency and publishes its case database. The pairing exists on this board to keep the national-office row honest: 'a country has an office' is not one fact but at least three different institutional arrangements, and Peru is the least documented of them. desc: Peru is one of a small group of states that has maintained an official military office for investigating anomalous aerial phenomena. The Fuerza Aérea del Perú office was reopened in 2013-2014 after a period of dormancy, a development the BBC covered on 5 February 2014 under the headline 'Por qué Perú reabrió la oficina de búsqueda de ovnis'. The Peruvian arrangement is a military rather than civil-aviation model, distinguishing it from Chile's DGAC-hosted SEFAA and France's CNES-hosted GEIPAN, and it is the least documented of the Latin American offices in English-language sources. It is included here as a placeholder with an honest statement of what is not yet established: the office's exact legal instrument, its current name and reporting line, its case output, and whether it publishes findings.
